en-US.title: My heart broke the moment I saw the deceased with their body severed | From Kim Yong-gyun to Jeon...
en-US.description:
Labor Day. It is a day to remember the lives and deaths of workers together.

Lee So-sun, a woman who lived her entire life as a mother to workers after the death of her son, who set himself on fire in protest of the Labor Standards Act. Kim Yong-gyun, a 24-year-old man who died while inspecting a conveyor belt alone after being subcontracted upon subcontracting. Their deaths were honored with state funerals, a collective mourning by society. We met Master Funeral Director Park Jae-ik, a man who was always with them on their final journey.

He was, in fact, a tailor at Pyeonghwa Market, just like Jeon Tae-il, and a member of the Cheonggye Garment Workers' Union. Now, he performs the work of washing and dressing the bodies of workers who died unjustly with his own hands before sending them off. What is the meaning of the labor involved in sending off deceased workers? How does that death save those left behind?

Check out the special story of Funeral Director Park Jae-ik in the video.

These include career gaps caused by treatment and prejudice regarding their medical history. Young cancer survivors interviewed during the reporting process stated, "Finding a job is harder than treatment."

For young cancer survivors, work is not merely an economic activity. It is a pathway to lift spirits dampened by the illness and reconnect with society. However, the path back to society after treatment is said to be far more difficult than expected.

Why is the door to returning to society still so narrow, even after they have recovered by overcoming the fear that things might go wrong? To hear their stories, we have gathered young people who have experienced cancer.
